transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Derek Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (OrionWave Head of Cloud Partnerships), Ethan Morales (OrionWave Infra), Lena Karam (OrionWave BizDev)

Summary:
Quick partner intro between Redwood and OrionWave to explore GPU orchestration integration and reseller/ISV channel fit. Primary topics: runbook for on-prem and cloud GPU routing, compatibility with OrionWave's multi-tenant pools, security/compliance needs, go-to-market motions, and a follow-up technical deep dive focused on perf baselines.

Topics covered:
- Partner model (reseller vs integration)
- Compatibility: Docker/k8s, node-level drivers, CUDA vs ROCm, TF/Torch inference runtimes
- Private deployments and VPC peering
- Benchmarks: p95 latency, tokens/sec, batch sizing
- Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM key handling
- Commercial: revenue split, onboarding timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the partnerships team at Redwood. We've got Derek, our solutions eng, and I'm going to hand it to him in a minute for the technical overview. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya Rao: Good, thanks Maya. Excited to chat — we had a look at the partner page and some of the bench notes.
[00:11] Lena Karam: hi all, quick intro from me — i'm looking after channel partnerships and go-to-market.
[00:15] Derek Patel: Cool. I'll do a quick run-through of what Redwood does from a runtime perspective and then we can map to where OrionWave sits. So, at a high level, Redwood provides hosted inference API, reserved/dedicated capacity, and a private deploy option for customers who need VPC/on-prem isolation. We optimize KV cache, batching, quantization aware paths, etc.
[00:31] Ethan Morales: Can I pause — when you say "private deploy" do you mean an on-prem appliance or like a software bundle we run in our customers' tenants?
[00:37] Derek Patel: Great callout. We have both flavors — a customer-managed control plane with a package you can deploy in their VPC, and an on-prem installer for fully air-gapped environments. For partners like you, the common pattern is we ship a partner-integration SDK that hooks into your orchestration plane and allows routing policies.
[00:48] Priya Rao: So, from OrionWave's side, we operate a multi-tenant GPU cloud that can be resold by systems integrators. We also have a managed offering where customers bring their own models and we host them on our fleet. Interest is twofold: 1) can Redwood sit on top of our stack as the inference control plane, and 2) if so, how does the economics and support model look.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Yep that's exactly the sort of thing we do with partners. We usually have two tracks: a tight integration where we expose routing and model variants to your control plane, or a reseller program where you run Redwood Dedicated instances on your infra and we provide the runtime/updates. Both are viable depending on commercials.
[01:21] Ethan Morales: technical — how opinionated is your runtime about the underlying drivers? For example we have a mix of Ampere NVIDIA and some upcoming ROCm nodes.
[01:29] Derek Patel: Good question. We compile kernels per hardware and prefer vendor drivers for best perf. Historically we've optimized overwhelmingly for CUDA/ampere but we've had customers using ROCm variants; there are some model-compat differences, and quantization paths need tuning. We can supply a compatibility matrix; I'll follow up with exact CUDA/ROCm supported versions.
[01:44] [crosstalk] Priya Rao: And autoscaling — can Redwood respect our node-level autoscale signals so we don't get double scaled?
[01:48] Derek Patel: Yes, we can. We integrate with Kubernetes node labels and autoscaler hooks. We typically recommend a thin adapter layer in your orchestration. That adapter exposes capacity signals and lets us do polite backpressure.
[02:00] Maya Chen: From a business standpoint — do you have any target verticals or customer size you'd prioritize for a first pilot?
[02:05] Lena Karam: We're seeing demand from fintech and media customers that need low-latency inference and local data residency. Those are good pilot targets.
[02:12] Priya Rao: Timeline — ideally we'd position a pilot in Q4. But internal legal wants SOC2, SAML SSO, and a network diagram before we go to customers.
[02:21] Derek Patel: We can provide our SOC2 report and our SAML SSO integration notes. For network diagrams, we have a partner network guide. I'll attach those.
[02:28] Ethan Morales: About performance — what do typical p95 latencies look like for e.g., a 4k context LLM? We run workloads that are sensitive to 150-200ms at p95.
[02:37] Derek Patel: For 4k sequences, depends on model family and quantization. If you're running a trimmed 2.7B variant quantized at int8 on Ampere A10/30 class, p95 is often in the 120-220ms ballpark with modest batching. For larger dense models it's higher. We'll need to run a baseline using your fleet to give a precise number.
[02:55] Priya Rao: Okay, that aligns. The other question — how do you handle model fallbacks and routing? If a node is constrained do you route to a smaller model or to a different region?
[03:04] Derek Patel: We have routing policies that can do region fallback, model variant fallback, and capacity tier fallback. It's policy driven — you can set latency SLOs, cost limits, and where to degrade to.
[03:13] Maya Chen: Also worth noting we do prefix cache and KV cache to reduce per-token latency and cost for repeated prompts — big for applications with repeated user context.
[03:21] Ethan Morales: Security — what's your stance on KMS? Customers want keys not leaving their VPC.
[03:25] Derek Patel: For private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integration. For hosted APIs we have envelope encryption but partners often prefer private deploy for full key ownership.
[03:35] Priya Rao: Sounds good. On the commercial side, what's an example revenue share for a reseller program?
[03:40] Maya Chen: That varies by commit and support level. Typical starter splits are in the 70/30 range to the partner for resale with a technical support overlay, but that gets negotiated based on commit and go-to-market co-sales. We'll send template terms.
[03:52] Lena Karam: are there minimums or ramp commitments?
[03:56] Maya Chen: For Dedicated/reseller, there's often a quarterly min to cover reserved capacity. For integration-only partners there's no strict min, it's more usage-driven.
[04:05] [pause] Derek Patel: One technical item I want to flag — model packaging. If you're running clients who bring their own models, we need model artifacts in a particular format and sometimes conversion scripts for optimized kernels. We'll share a sample converter and model packager.
[04:18] Ethan Morales: Do you have an existing partner SDK for control plane hooks?
[04:21] Derek Patel: Yes, a lightweight SDK and a webhook pattern. It supports routing decisions, capacity reports, and a plugin for our operator that runs in k8s. We also provide a REST fallback.
[04:30] Priya Rao: Great. One of our legal asks is data residency and logs — can you granularly control what telemetry we or our customers see?
[04:38] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We have token-level tracing and you can opt into only aggregated metrics or full traces. For partners we usually set up an isolated telemetry bucket with redacted user PII.
[04:47] Ethan Morales: Okay. Proposed next step for us is to see a technical runbook and share our node specs so Derek can draft perf tests.
[04:54] Derek Patel: I'll take that. Also I'll include a perf-run checklist with sample prompts and synthetic traces.
[05:00] [30 minute mark summary — speakers recap plan]
[30:05] Maya Chen: To recap: Redwood will send partner program deck, SOC2 + security pack, SDK links, and perf-run checklist. OrionWave will send fleet topology, node specs, and a list of pilot customers. We'll aim to schedule the technical deep dive the week of Aug 12.
[30:20] Priya Rao: That works, appreciate it.
[30:23] Lena Karam: Quick commercial question — are there marketing co-funds for pilot customers?
[30:27] Maya Chen: We have co-marketing credits and joint case study templates for pilots that reach production. We'll include that in the partnership brief.
[30:33] Ethan Morales: One last technical: we sometimes use spot/preemptible GPUs. Does Redwood support preemptible fleets gracefully?
[30:40] Derek Patel: Yes, we support preemptible capacity but we recommend combining it with fallback routing and warm standby instances to avoid p95 spikes. We'll show sample policies.
[30:50] [some cross talk and brief clarification]
[31:10] Priya Rao: ok great. I'm tagging Ethan and Lena — we'll align internally and get back to you with proposed pilot customers.
[31:16] Maya Chen: Thanks, everyone. We'll send the package and proposed times.
[31:20] Derek Patel: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription artifacts: occasional name mis-hears (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate" instead of "Redwood Dedicated"), timestamps were approximate, some crosstalk at 01:44 and 30:50, and a few trimmed filler words.
